strengths: Conceptual formulation: Casting symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching over Lie group orbits is elegant and provides a principled bridge between continuous generative modeling (CFM) and geometric learning.

Insightful analysis of failure modes: The paper identifies and thoroughly analyzes the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon—where the symmetric arrangement of target modes causes intermediate velocities to cancel out until late in the flow trajectory. The empirical analysis of posterior entropy (Section 5.4 and Appendix D) is clear and illuminating.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluation: The method is validated quantitatively against LieGAN using Wasserstein-1 distance on both 2D and 3D datasets, showing clear improvements on the tested benchmarks.

Honesty regarding limitations: The authors explicitly document where the method struggles (e.g., the failure on the octahedral group under uniform schedules, and persistent failure on the icosahedral group even with the skewed schedule).
weaknesses: Synthetic and low-dimensional evaluation only: Experiments are entirely confined to simple synthetic point clouds (e.g., canonical 2D arrows, single irregular tetrahedra, and four simple multi-object shapes). The paper does not evaluate on standard real-world geometric benchmarks (e.g., ModelNet, ScanObjectNN) or physical/molecular systems (e.g., N-body, QM9), leaving real-world applicability unproven.

Limited comparative baselines: The empirical comparison is conducted only against LieGAN (Yang et al., 2023). Several other related methods for symmetry/group learning cited in the paper (e.g., Allingham et al., 2024; Karjol et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024; Shaw et al., 2024) are not benchmarked.

Heuristic solution to mode convergence: The proposed power-law time-skewing schedule ($p(t) \propto t^{n-1}$) is an ad-hoc heuristic that relieves the symptom for order-24 Octahedral symmetry but fails to generalize to order-60 Icosahedral symmetry, showing that the underlying structural issue of velocity cancellation in CFM remains fundamentally open.

Assumption of synthetic group action setup: The training framework generates pairs $(x_0, x_1)$ by explicitly sampling $g \sim p(G)$ and applying $x_0 = g x_1$. In real-world unstructured symmetry discovery, datasets are typically unordered observations where clean paired orbits under a known compact hypothesis group are not readily accessible without substantial noise and nuisance variations.

strengths: Original and elegant formulation: Casting the unsupervised discovery of unknown continuous and discrete symmetry subgroups as conditional flow matching over Lie groups/algebras from a broader hypothesis group.

Insightful analysis of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon: The paper clearly explains and empirically demonstrates why flow matching struggles with symmetric discrete targets—namely, equidistant symmetric target modes cause the conditional expectations of Lie algebra velocities to cancel out near $t=0$, keeping trajectories stationary until late timesteps.

The proposed power-law time scheduling provides a simple and effective mitigation: By skewing time sampling towards $t=1$, the method successfully recovers the 24-element octahedral group SO(3) $\to$ Oct, where uniform time sampling failed completely.

Comprehensive visualization and clear presentation: The manuscript and appendix provide extensive visual evidence, including trajectory analysis, Euler angle Mollweide projections, and step-by-step point cloud evolutions.
weaknesses: Synthetic and limited experimental scope: The evaluation is restricted to clean, canonical synthetic point clouds (e.g., 2D arrows, 3D irregular tetrahedra/polyhedra). It lacks validation on standard real-world or semi-realistic symmetry discovery benchmarks (e.g., rotated MNIST, QM9 molecular geometries, or ModelNet objects) where data exhibits intra-class variation, noise, or partial observations.

Limited baseline comparisons: The empirical comparison is only conducted against LieGAN (Yang et al., 2023). Important recent baselines for discrete and continuous symmetry discovery (e.g., Allingham et al., 2024; Karjol et al., 2024; Benton et al., 2020) are discussed in related work but omitted from the quantitative evaluation.

Scalability bottlenecks: The method fails on higher-order subgroups like the icosahedral group (60 elements) even with the power schedule, collapsing to identity transforms. Scalability to larger groups, non-compact groups, or higher-dimensional spaces remains an unaddressed challenge.

Downstream utility is not demonstrated: The paper does not show whether the discovered symmetries can be successfully integrated into downstream equivariant architectures or used for invariant representation learning.

strengths: Original and elegant formulation: Framing symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching over a Lie group manifold to transport a broad prior distribution towards the data-supported subgroup is conceptually novel.

Insightful analysis of 'last-minute mode convergence': The authors clearly analyze why flow matching encounters difficulties with highly symmetric target distributions (the conditional vector fields cancel out near t=0, keeping the posterior entropy nearly uniform until late timesteps).

Unified treatment of continuous and discrete symmetries: The framework handles continuous subgroups (SO(2)), discrete subgroups (C4, Tet), and demonstrates an interesting trick of performing flow matching over the complex domain (GL(2, C)) to capture reflection symmetries in D4.

Clear visual presentation: The figures and trajectory visualizations (e.g., Mollweide projections, vector field portraits, and centroid paths) provide clear intuitive understanding of the model's behavior during generation.
weaknesses: Overly synthetic and limited evaluation: Experiments are strictly restricted to canonical 2D/3D toy point clouds (single 2D arrows and 3D irregular tetrahedra with no measurement noise). The paper does not evaluate on standard symmetry discovery benchmarks (e.g., rotated MNIST, QM9, dynamical physical systems, or ModelNet).

Limited baseline comparisons: The method is only compared against a single baseline, LieGAN (Yang et al., 2023). Other relevant prior and concurrent works on continuous or discrete symmetry discovery (e.g., Allingham et al., 2024; Karjol et al., 2024; Shaw et al., 2024) are discussed in the related work but omitted from experimental comparison.

Scalability bottlenecks to moderately sized groups: The model already struggles on the Octahedral group (order 24) under uniform time sampling, requiring an ad-hoc power time schedule. Even with this schedule, it fails completely on the Icosahedral group (order 60), collapsing to predicting only the identity. This reveals fundamental limitations in scalability for groups with denser orbits.

No downstream validation: The paper does not demonstrate the practical utility of the discovered symmetries, such as informing equivariant network architectures, improving sample efficiency in invariant prediction tasks, or serving as a data augmentation policy.

Lack of automated group identification: Algorithm 3 generates individual transformed samples/group elements, but the method does not provide a formal mechanism to identify the abstract subgroup structure (e.g., determining group generators, order, or algebraic presentation) directly from the generated distribution without manual inspection.

strengths: Novel and conceptually elegant formulation: Reframing symmetry discovery as distribution support learning on a Lie group via flow matching is intuitive and effectively bypasses the instability of adversarial approaches (like LieGAN) and the need for handcrafted generator bases.

Unified framework for both continuous and discrete symmetries: Most prior methods are heavily tailored toward either continuous Lie groups or discrete/finite groups. LieFlow discovers both continuous (e.g., SO(2)) and discrete subgroups (e.g., C4, Tet, Oct, Ico) without changing the core objective or requiring specialized priors.

Insightful diagnosis of 'last-minute mode convergence': The authors identify that flow matching toward discrete symmetric modes induces near-zero vector fields early in time due to vector cancellation. The mathematical and empirical analysis in Section 5.4 and Appendix D, along with the power time scheduling solution, is well-reasoned and effective.

Thorough experimental validation: The paper covers synthetic 2D/3D shapes, diverse ground truth symmetry groups, non-compact hypothesis groups (GL(2)+), partial symmetries, and perturbed/masked real-world objects (ModelNet10), consistently outperforming LieGAN on discrete subgroups.
weaknesses: Controlled and synthetic data generation: In both synthetic benchmarks and ModelNet10, the symmetry in the data is synthetically injected by applying exact group transformations to canonical shapes. Evaluating on natural datasets exhibiting inherent, non-exact, or noisy physical/geometric symmetries would strengthen the empirical significance.

Lack of downstream task evaluation: The introduction motivates symmetry discovery through inductive biases for equivariant neural networks, but the paper does not demonstrate using the learned symmetries to improve sample efficiency or performance on a downstream predictive task.

Scalability to higher-dimensional or general non-compact groups: The method assumes a known ambient hypothesis Lie group G with a tractable exponential/logarithm map. Scaling to higher dimensions or general non-compact Lie groups (beyond 2x2 matrices) remains challenging and is left largely as future work.

strengths: Novel and conceptually elegant formulation: Reframing symmetry discovery as learning a probability distribution on a Lie group via flow matching shifts the paradigm away from brittle generator estimation or adversarial training to a stable, regression-based support-learning problem.

Unified treatment of continuous and discrete symmetries: Unlike prior works (e.g., LieGAN) that require specialized prior distributions or are restricted to either discrete or continuous symmetries, LieFlow models both continuous subgroups and discrete subgroups within the same framework.

Insightful analysis of 'last-minute convergence': The paper clearly explains why discrete subgroups induce near-zero velocity fields until late in the flow (due to vector cancellation among symmetric target modes) and effectively mitigates this with a tailored power time schedule.

Thorough empirical validation: The method is validated on 2D synthetic point clouds, 3D synthetic shapes, and ModelNet10, successfully handling partial observations, high-order discrete groups (Icosahedral), and noisy/masked point clouds, consistently outperforming LieGAN.
weaknesses: Reliance on a prescribed hypothesis group: The method assumes the target group $H$ is a subgroup of a known, tractable Lie group $G$ (e.g., $SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)$). While broader than assuming $H$ directly, it still requires domain expertise to select an appropriate hypothesis group and metric.

Synthetic symmetry generation setup: In the experiments on ModelNet10, data is generated by applying group actions from $H$ to canonical objects. While standard in the symmetry discovery literature, it remains somewhat artificial compared to natural datasets with non-uniform or noisy orbit distributions.

Lack of quantitative comparisons to other recent baselines: While LieGAN (Yang et al., 2023) is a strong and relevant baseline, other recent related approaches (such as Allingham et al., 2024 for generative symmetry models or Karjol et al., 2024 for discrete symmetries) are only discussed qualitatively without direct empirical comparisons.

Absence of explicit algebraic extraction: The framework outputs samples from the learned distribution $p_\theta(g)$ over $G$, but does not provide an automated mechanism (e.g., clustering or group table synthesis) to output the formal discrete group presentation or closed-form generators.

strengths: Formulating symmetry discovery as conditional distribution learning over a Lie group via flow matching is a clean and conceptually appealing framework that bridges generative modeling and geometric deep learning.

Unlike prior Lie algebra generator-learning methods (e.g., LieGAN) which rely on unimodal/Gaussian coefficient priors and struggle with discrete subgroups, LieFlow naturally captures both continuous and discrete symmetries within a unified formulation.

The identification of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups—where velocity fields cancel out across symmetric modes early in the trajectory—provides valuable conceptual insight into flow matching dynamics on groups, and the proposed power time schedule offers a simple and effective mitigation.

The empirical results demonstrate substantial quantitative and qualitative improvements over LieGAN across 2D and 3D synthetic point clouds and rotated ModelNet10, particularly on discrete symmetry groups (e.g., tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral).
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation relies on synthetically generated symmetries: objects are explicitly rotated by ground-truth group actions to create orbits, rather than discovering intrinsic or latent symmetries naturally occurring in real-world data distributions (e.g., molecular trajectories, dynamical physical systems, or natural image manifolds).

Empirical comparisons are restricted to a single baseline (LieGAN). Including comparisons against other recent symmetry discovery frameworks (e.g., finite group discovery methods or invariant/equivariant representation learning baselines) would provide a stronger benchmark of the method's standing.

The framework requires specifying a compact or tractable ambient hypothesis Lie group G upfront. As demonstrated by the significant performance degradation when moving from SO(2) to GL(2)+ (Table 1), performance is sensitive to the choice of prior group parameterization and sampling distribution.

The paper lacks downstream validation showing how the discovered symmetry groups can be directly leveraged to build equivariant architectures or improve sample efficiency on practical predictive tasks.

strengths: Novel and elegant conceptual formulation: Reframing symmetry discovery as learning a probability distribution on a Lie group via flow matching is an insightful shift away from traditional generator estimation or adversarial training.

Unified framework for discrete and continuous symmetries: LieFlow naturally recovers both continuous subgroups (e.g., SO(2)) and finite discrete subgroups (e.g., C4, tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral) without needing prior knowledge of the subgroup type or handcrafted prior mixtures.

Insightful analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon: The authors clearly identify and formalize the challenge of learning discrete subgroups with flow matching—where symmetric velocity vectors cancel out until t approaches 1—and propose an effective power time-scheduling strategy to resolve it.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The method is evaluated across 2D/3D synthetic datasets, real-world object point clouds (ModelNet10), partially observed symmetries, noisy settings, and real-world human motion data (MI-Motion), consistently outperforming strong baselines like LieGAN and SGM.
weaknesses: Dependence on the hypothesis group G: The method requires prescribing a hypothesis Lie group in advance (e.g., SO(2), GL(2), SO(3)), and scaling to higher-dimensional or non-compact matrix Lie groups remains non-trivial due to logarithm branch cuts and sampling complexity.

Lack of explicit algebraic presentation: LieFlow produces an empirical distribution and sampler over group transformations rather than extracting explicit algebraic generators, requiring post-processing or clustering before integration into downstream equivariant architectures.

Strong theoretical assumptions: Theorem B.4 requires ideal convergence on the data support and assumes point stabilizers are global symmetries (Assumption B.3), which may not hold for objects with continuous self-symmetries or noisy real-world data distributions.

Inference latency: Generating transformations requires multi-step numerical ODE integration (Euler integration over Lie algebra increments), which can be computationally slower at test time compared to closed-form or single-pass generator evaluations.

strengths: Novel and conceptually elegant formulation: Reframing symmetry discovery as a conditional flow matching problem directly over a hypothesis Lie group acting on the data space is a clean, principled paradigm shift away from adversarial Lie algebra estimation or explicit prototype canonization.

Unified framework for discrete and continuous symmetries: Unlike prior approaches (such as LieGAN) that require specialized priors (e.g., multi-modal delta mixtures) to capture discrete subgroups, LieFlow naturally discovers continuous subgroups (SO(2)), discrete point groups (Tet, Oct, Ico, C4), and partially observed symmetries within a single architecture.

Insightful analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon: Section 5.4 and Appendix E provide a clear mathematical and intuitive explanation of why discrete symmetry learning experiences cancellation of conditional velocity fields at small t (due to mode symmetry), along with an effective power time-scheduling solution.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates strong quantitative improvements over competitive baselines (LieGAN, SGM, Augerino) across synthetic 2D/3D datasets, ModelNet10, and real-world human motion data (MI-Motion), supported by robust noise analyses and ablation studies.

Theoretical grounding: Appendix B provides clear conditions (ideal convergence, globally generated support, trivial/global point stabilizers) under which the support of the learned distribution is guaranteed to concentrate on the true symmetry subgroup H.
weaknesses: Dependence on hypothesis group specification: The method requires specifying an ambient Lie group G containing the true symmetry H a priori. While common in symmetry discovery, performance and tractability on higher-dimensional, non-compact, or unknown ambient groups (beyond SO(2), GL(2), and SO(3)) remain untested.

Distribution support vs. explicit group presentation: LieFlow outputs empirical transformation samples whose support reveals H, but does not extract explicit algebraic representations (e.g., generators, group order, or irreducible representations), which limits direct plug-and-play integration into steerable equivariant neural network architectures.

Sensitivity to continuous point stabilizers: As discussed in Appendix A, if individual data points have continuous self-symmetries (e.g., surfaces of revolution under SO(3)), the infinitesimal action map J_xt has a non-trivial kernel, making the Lie algebra regression target unidentifiable without additional gauge fixing or quotient formulation.
Baseline coverage on real-world data: On the MI-Motion benchmark, the comparison is limited solely to LieGAN, omitting comparisons with other recent unsupervised symmetry discovery methods.

strengths: Novel Conceptual Framing: Reframing symmetry discovery as a distribution learning / support recovery problem over a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching is conceptually clean, principled, and elegant.

Unified Treatment of Continuous and Discrete Symmetries: Unlike prior works such as LieGAN (which requires pre-specifying modal delta priors to capture discrete subgroups) or infinitesimal generator methods (which cannot handle discrete groups), LieFlow discovers both continuous and discrete subgroups within a single unified framework.

Insightful Analysis of 'Last-Minute Mode Convergence': The paper identifies and analyzes a specific failure mode when applying flow matching to discrete subgroups—vector field cancellation causing near-zero drift until $t \approx 1$. The theoretical/empirical analysis of posterior entropy and the proposed skewed power time schedule provide a well-motivated and effective remedy.

Rigorous Formulation: The mathematical formulation directly predicts Lie algebra elements along orbit paths and clearly delineates the necessary conditions on stabilizers for identifiability (e.g., trivial infinitesimal stabilizer), supported by formal propositions in Appendix B.

Thorough Experimental Validation: The method is comprehensively evaluated on synthetic 2D/3D shapes, 3D ModelNet10, and real-world human motion capture (MI-Motion), demonstrating convincing quantitative improvements (Wasserstein-1 distance and relative improvement) over competitive baselines like LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino.
weaknesses: Dependency on Hypothesis Group: LieFlow requires specifying a hypothesis group $G$ that contains the target symmetry $H$. As discussed in the limitations, if $G$ is chosen to be overly broad or high-dimensional, sampling and optimization can become significantly more difficult, limiting applicability when candidate groups are entirely unknown.

Sampling vs. Explicit Algebraic Extraction: LieFlow outputs a learned empirical distribution over group elements (via accumulated transformations) rather than an explicit algebraic presentation (such as discrete group generators, relations, or Lie algebra bases). Downstream tasks must rely on clustering or post-processing to obtain symbolic/algebraic forms.

Evaluation on Semi-Synthetic Benchmarks: For both synthetic objects and ModelNet10, the symmetries are synthetically injected by applying group actions $H$ to canonical objects. While MI-Motion provides an organic test case, it only exhibits a relatively simple vertical $C_4$ yaw symmetry; validation on more complex natural physical or molecular symmetries would strengthen empirical significance.

Scalability to Higher-Dimensional Groups: Experiments are restricted to low-dimensional matrix Lie groups ($SO(2)$, $GL(2)$, $SO(3)$). The behavior and computational tractability of the Lie algebra regression and matrix exponential accumulation in higher dimensions (e.g., $SE(3)$, $SO(N)$ for $N > 3$) remain unexplored.
